summary: Gives IAB and IESG recommendations to the address registries on assigning IPv6 blocks to end sites, such as /48 in general. It was replaced by RFC 6177.

eli5.summary: It tells the address givers how big a chunk of addresses to hand each home or business.

questions: how large an ipv6 block for a site
how much ipv6 address space for a site
subtitle: Recommendations for how large an IPv6 address block to give to end sites.

tldr.problem: IPv6 address space is vastly larger than IPv4, but ISPs and registries still needed guidance on how much to assign to each home, business, or organization. The assignment strategy affects network renumbering costs, routing efficiency, and whether sites can grow without asking for more addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB and IESG recommend a fixed boundary at /48 for most sites (giving each site 2^16 subnets), /64 for single-subnet scenarios, and /128 for single devices. This uniform approach allows sites to maintain the same internal numbering structure even if they change ISPs, and simplifies DNS and routing.
tldr.outcome: The /48 recommendation has become the foundation of IPv6 site planning. It provides enough space for any organization to grow internally and provides stability if the organization changes providers. RFC 6177 later updated these recommendations.

today: RFC 3177 provides the foundational IPv6 allocation policy. The /48 recommendation became the basis for site allocation across most of the world. RFC 6177 later updated and refined these recommendations, adjusting guidance for residential users and other specific cases while maintaining the /48 as the standard allocation.

sections.title: The IPv6 Allocation Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 has an address space orders of magnitude larger than IPv4, but the question of how to allocate it efficiently and fairly remains. The key issue is the boundary between the public Internet topology (managed by ISPs and registries) and the private topology of individual sites (homes, offices, enterprises). How much address space should a site receive?

Unlike IPv4, where addresses are scarce and must be allocated sparingly, IPv6 has enough space to be generous. At the same time, careful stewardship is important to avoid making routing tables unwieldy. The RFC is primarily a recommendation from the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) to the Regional Internet Registries (RIRs: APNIC, ARIN, and RIPE-NCC) on how to balance these concerns.

The document refines an earlier IAB/IESG statement from September 2000 and provides the historical record of the reasoning behind the allocation policy that would shape IPv6 networks for decades.
sections.eli5: When the Internet grew to need IPv6, people had to decide: how many addresses should we give a house, a small company, or a big company? This RFC gives the answer.

sections.title: Why /48 Makes Sense
sections.content:
The IPv6 address is 128 bits, split into 64 bits for the network and 64 bits for hosts (or subnets and hosts). When an ISP assigns a prefix to a site, the question is where to split the assignment: give them a /48, /64, or something else?

The RFC argues for a uniform /48 boundary for most sites. A /48 prefix leaves 48 bits for the ISP to assign, and the site owns the remaining 80 bits (48 for subnets under the /48, 32 for hosts within each subnet). This is enormous: a /48 gives a site 2^16 subnets (65,536), each with 2^64 hosts. Even a massive enterprise will never need more.

The advantage of a fixed boundary is that if a site changes ISPs, it can renumber using the same internal subnetting structure: the site can use the same subnet numbers under each new prefix it receives. Without a fixed boundary, a site that receives /47 from one ISP and a /49 from another would need to maintain two different subnet numbering schemes or renumber to fit both under the smallest prefix, creating complexity.

The RFC also notes that the 64/64 split (64 bits for network, 64 for hosts) is built into many IPv6 standards, including address autoconfiguration (which places a locally unique 64-bit number in the host part) and EUI-64 addressing. A /48 preserves this structure while giving sites flexibility.
sections.eli5: IPv6 is so big that you can safely give everyone a /48 and still have plenty left. And by being consistent—everyone gets /48—you avoid confusion when sites change providers.

sections.title: The Recommended Allocation Tiers
sections.content:
The RFC recommends three tiers of allocation:

/48 for the general case. Homes, small businesses, and large enterprises should all receive a /48. This provides massive internal flexibility and eliminates the burden on ISPs and registries of judging each site's growth plans. With a /48, even a very large enterprise can provision internal subnets, migrate between providers, and support multiple business units without requesting more address space.

/64 for single-subnet scenarios. When it is known that exactly one subnet is needed—for example, a mobile device such as a phone with one additional network interface (Bluetooth or 802.11)—a /64 is sufficient. A /64 gives 2^64 individual addresses within a single subnet, which is more than enough for any device.

/128 for single devices. When a single device is connecting (such as a PC dialing in via PPP), a /128 (a single address) may be assigned, typically as part of a larger /64 prefix shared among multiple dial-in users.

The RFC also notes that very large subscribers could receive a /47 or shorter prefix, or even multiple /48s, but this is the exception rather than the rule.
sections.eli5: Most places get a /48 (huge). A phone with one network gets a /64 (still huge). A single device gets a /128 (just one address). Easy.

sections.title: Will /48 Allocations Exhaust the Space?
sections.content:
The RFC addresses the concern head-on: is giving every site a /48 wasteful? The answer is no, with detailed analysis. Under the 001 Global Unicast Address prefix (which covers most of the current IPv6 allocation), there are 45 variable bits, allowing for 2^45 different /48 prefixes. That is about 35 trillion /48s.

Using the "H ratio" from RFC 1715 (a measure of address space allocation efficiency), the RFC calculates that an H ratio of 0.25 (the threshold where problems start to appear) would allow for 178 billion /48 prefixes. To put this in perspective, the projected world population in 2050 is about 10 billion people. Even at 80 bits of address space per person (an "extremely ambitious scaling goal"), there is no risk of exhaustion.

The RFC also notes that the IETF has reserved more than 85% of the IPv6 address space for future use. Should allocation policies need to change in the future, that reserved space is available without requiring a new version of IP.
sections.eli5: There are so many /48s that you could give one to every person on Earth and still have enough left over. Do not worry about running out.

sections.title: Multihoming and Provider Independence
sections.content:
One important implication of /48 allocation is support for multihoming—when a site connects to multiple ISPs simultaneously. In IPv4, this is done by having the same prefix advertised by multiple ISPs, but this causes routing table growth. In IPv6, the ideal approach is for each ISP to give the site a prefix, and for the site to advertise all of them.

If prefixes have different lengths (one ISP gives a /47, another a /49), the site must either maintain different internal subnetting structures or renumber to fit both under a single (smaller) prefix. With a uniform /48 boundary, the site can use the same internal subnetting under each prefix, simplifying operation and DNS configuration.

A fixed prefix boundary also enables provider-independent addressing: if a site receives multiple /48s and advertises them all to the Internet, then changing one ISP does not require renumbering the addresses from other ISPs, making it easier to transition between providers.
sections.eli5: If a business uses two Internet providers, it can get a /48 from each one and use them both without renumbering. That is power and flexibility.
